rows.statement: Everything you can touch, and the air around you, is made of atoms.
rows.explanation: Solids, liquids and gases are all made of atoms. Even air is.

rows.statement: Light and heat are made of atoms, just like a rock is.
rows.explanation: Light and heat are not matter. They are not made of atoms.

rows.statement: Every atom has a tiny centre called the nucleus, with electrons around it.
rows.explanation: The nucleus sits in the middle and the electrons are around it.

rows.statement: Neutrons have a negative charge.
rows.explanation: Neutrons have no charge. Electrons are the negative ones.

rows.statement: Protons are positive, electrons are negative, and neutrons have no charge.
rows.explanation: These three charges are what each particle of an atom is like.

rows.statement: If an atom gains a neutron, it becomes a different element.
rows.explanation: The number of protons decides the element. A different number of neutrons only makes a different isotope.

rows.statement: The number of protons in an atom tells you which element it is.
rows.explanation: Every carbon atom has 6 protons and every oxygen atom has 8.

rows.statement: An isotope is always radioactive.
rows.explanation: Many isotopes are perfectly stable. An isotope is not automatically radioactive.

rows.statement: Isotopes of one element have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
rows.explanation: Same protons means same element. Different neutrons means a different isotope.

rows.statement: Every nucleus is unstable and will change one day.
rows.explanation: Some nuclei stay the same for ever. Only unstable ones can change.

rows.statement: Radioactivity is something people invented in the last hundred years.
rows.explanation: Radioactivity was here long before people. It is a natural process.

rows.statement: Rocks, air, food and even your own body contain a little natural radioactivity.
rows.explanation: Natural radioactivity is all around us, and inside us.

rows.statement: Radioactive always means dangerous.
rows.explanation: It depends on the kind and the amount. Radioactive does not automatically mean dangerous.

rows.statement: An unstable nucleus changes all by itself, and nobody can say exactly when one nucleus will change.
rows.explanation: The change is natural and unpredictable for a single nucleus.

rows.statement: An unstable nucleus has to be hit by something before it can decay.
rows.explanation: Natural decay needs no push. The nucleus changes on its own.

rows.statement: Alpha, beta and gamma are three different kinds of radiation.
rows.explanation: They come out of a changing nucleus, but they are three different things.

rows.statement: Alpha, beta and gamma are just three names for the same thing.
rows.explanation: They are different from each other. That is why they have different names.

rows.statement: Half-life is about a crowd of nuclei, not a timer inside each atom.
rows.explanation: In a big group, half of the unstable nuclei change in one half-life. You cannot say which ones.

rows.statement: After one half-life, all the radioactive nuclei in a sample are gone.
rows.explanation: After one half-life, half of them are left, not none.

rows.statement: In a decay chain, every change makes a different nucleus, and nothing simply vanishes.
rows.explanation: One decay is not always the end. The new nucleus can change again.
